title: Tahir Hussain
text: I’m Tahir Hussain, a Master of Data Science student at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver. I grew up in Dewas, Madhya Pradesh, India, and completed my B.Tech. in Electronics and Communication Engineering with a minor in Computer Science at NIT Jalandhar. Before joining UBC, I worked as a Software Engineer at Paytm, where I primarily worked on backend systems and data-intensive applications. I am now looking to build on my software engineering experience with stronger skills in statistics, data science, and machine learning, and use them to solve real-world problems.

title: Using R and Python in One Document
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER, released under the CC0 licence. Cite as Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). I use the copy that ships inside the palmerpenguins R package, so nothing is downloaded when the site is built.
In this post I use R and Python in the same document. R prepares a summary of the penguin data, Python reads that summary and works with it, and then R reads a result that Python computed. The two languages talk to each other through the reticulate package.

title: Using R and Python in One Document
section: Set up R and point it at the project’s Python
text:
Set up R and point it at the project’s Python

library(reticulate)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

# Use the Python from this project's .venv (the post runs from its own folder)
use_virtualenv("../../.venv", required = TRUE)

title: Using R and Python in One Document
Using R and Python in One Document
section: Step 2: Python reads the R object
text:
Step 2: Python reads the R object
In Python, an R object is available as r.name. Here r.species_summary is the data frame from the chunk above, seen as a pandas DataFrame.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = r.species_summary.copy() # pyrefly: ignore
df["species"] = df["species"].astype(str)
df["mass_per_mm_flipper"] = (
    df["mean_body_mass_g"] / df["mean_flipper_length_mm"]
).round(2)

# Objects created here can be read back in R with py$name
python_summary = df
heaviest = str(df.loc[df["mean_body_mass_g"].idxmax(), "species"])

df

ax.bar(df["species"], df["mean_body_mass_g"])

plt.show()







Figure 1: Average body mass by species, drawn in Python from a summary computed in R.

title: Using R and Python in One Document
text:
What I found
Gentoo penguins are the heaviest species on average, and the bar chart and table agree. The main point of this post is the workflow: R did the data preparation, Python did the extra calculation and plotting, and R displayed the results, all in one document.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation day on campus.


Starting the Master of Data Science program at UBC has been a major change for me. A few weeks ago, I was still in India preparing for my move to Vancouver, and now I am attending classes at one of Canada’s largest universities. Arriving in Vancouver and seeing the UBC campus in person made the transition feel much more real. Orientation was a great opportunity to meet my classmates, learn more about the program, and get a better idea of what the next several months will look like.
The first couple of weeks have been a combination of excitement and adjustment. The program moves quickly, and there is a lot to learn across programming, computing platforms, data manipulation, and statistics. Coming from a software engineering background, some of the programming concepts feel familiar, but working with R and approaching problems from a statistical perspective has been a different experience for me. One of the biggest surprises has been how quickly we move from introducing a concept to actually applying it in labs and assignments.
After two weeks, I am still figuring out how to manage the pace, but I am enjoying the experience. There is definitely a lot to keep up with, but being surrounded by classmates with different academic and professional backgrounds makes the experience interesting. I know the coming months will be challenging, but I am looking forward to seeing how much I can learn and how my software engineering background can complement the data science skills I develop at UBC.

title: Penguins Data Processing with R
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER, released under the CC0 licence. Cite as Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). I use the copy that ships inside the palmerpenguins R package, so nothing is downloaded when the site is built.

Loading Packages

library(janitor)
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)



Loading the data

penguins_data <- penguins |>
  drop_na(species, sex, body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm)

head(penguins_data)

6 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181        3625
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>


The dataset contains measurements of penguins from three species: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. I removed rows with missing values in the variables used in this analysis.

head(clean_penguins_data)

Filtering Rows on Condition

filter_penguins_data <- clean_penguins_data |>
  filter(species == "Adelie")

head(filter_penguins_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
5 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
6 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181        3625
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>




Selecting Columns

subset_penguins_data <- filter_penguins_data |>
  select(species, island, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)

head(subset_penguins_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18  
4 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3
5 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6
6 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8




Comparing body mass by species
First, I calculate the average body mass for each species.

average_mass <- penguins_data |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g),
    median_body_mass_g = median(body_mass_g),
    n = n()
  )

average_mass

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species   mean_body_mass_g median_body_mass_g     n
  <fct>                <dbl>              <dbl> <int>
1 Adelie               3706.               3700   146
2 Chinstrap            3733.               3700    68
3 Gentoo               5092.               5050   119


The results show that body mass differs between the three species. Gentoo penguins have the highest average body mass, while Adelie penguins have the lowest average body mass.


Body mass and flipper length
Next, I examine the relationship between body mass and flipper length.

ggplot(
  penguins_data,
  aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Body mass and flipper length of Palmer Penguins by species.





The figure shows a positive relationship between flipper length and body mass: penguins with longer flippers generally tend to have greater body mass. The species also form somewhat distinct groups.


Comparing males and females
Finally, I compare the average body mass of male and female penguins.

sex_mass <- penguins_data |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarise(
    mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

sex_mass

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  species   sex    mean_body_mass_g
  <fct>     <fct>             <dbl>
1 Adelie    female            3369.
2 Adelie    male              4043.
3 Chinstrap female            3527.
4 Chinstrap male              3939.
5 Gentoo    female            4680.
6 Gentoo    male              5485.


Across the species, the average body mass differs between males and females. This provides another example of how biological characteristics can vary within and between penguin species.


Conclusion
Using the Palmer Penguins dataset, I found clear differences in body mass between species. Body mass is also positively related to flipper length, and average body mass differs between males and females. These simple summaries and visualizations demonstrate how R can be used to explore relationships in a real dataset.

title: Exploring Penguin Body Size with Python
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER, released under the CC0 licence. Cite as Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). I use the copy that ships inside the palmerpenguins Python package, so nothing is downloaded when the site is built.
The dataset has measurements for 344 penguins from three species: Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo. In this post I do the same kind of analysis as in my R post, but in Python with pandas and matplotlib. I ask how body mass differs between species, how it relates to flipper length, and how it differs between males and females.

penguins_data = penguins.dropna(

title: Exploring Penguin Body Size with Python
text:
Body mass and flipper length

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
for species, group in penguins_data.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(
        group["flipper_length_mm"],
        group["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.7,
    )
ax.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
ax.legend(title="Species")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Body mass and flipper length of Palmer Penguins by species.






corr = penguins_data["flipper_length_mm"].corr(penguins_data["body_mass_g"])
print(f"Correlation between flipper length and body mass: {corr:.2f}")

Correlation between flipper length and body mass: 0.87


The figure shows a strong positive relationship: penguins with longer flippers tend to be heavier. The correlation is about 0.87. The species also form fairly distinct groups, with Gentoo penguins in the top right.

title: Exploring Penguin Body Size with Python
text:
Conclusion
Using the Palmer Penguins data in Python, I found clear differences in body mass between species, a strong positive link between flipper length and body mass, and a consistent difference between the sexes. These simple summaries show how pandas and matplotlib can be used to explore a real dataset.

title: About
text:
I am from Dewas, a city in Madhya Pradesh, India. I completed my undergraduate degree in Electronics and Communication Engineering with a minor in Computer Science at Dr. B. R. Ambedkar National Institute of Technology, Jalandhar.
During university, I became increasingly interested in software development and problem solving. Although my undergraduate degree was in electronics and communication engineering, my minor in computer science and my projects gave me an opportunity to explore programming and software development more deeply.
After graduating, I joined Paytm as a Software Engineer after completing an internship there. title: About
text:
Why data science
My interest in data science grew from the intersection of software engineering and data. As a software engineer, I spent much of my time building systems that processed and moved data. Over time, I became more interested in the next question: what can we actually learn from that data, and how can it be used to make better decisions?
I chose the UBC Master of Data Science program because I wanted to develop a stronger foundation in areas that were not a major part of my previous work, particularly statistics, probability, data analysis, and machine learning. At the same time, the program allows me to build on the programming and software engineering skills I already have.
I am especially interested in the practical side of data science. Rather than focusing only on theory, I want to learn how to take a real-world problem, work with messy data, build an appropriate model or analysis, and communicate the results clearly.
In the long term, I hope to explore different areas of data science, machine learning, and artificial intelligence and find ways to combine these skills with my software engineering background.

title: About
text:
Outside of data science
Outside of my studies, I enjoy staying active and spending time outdoors. I regularly go to the gym and enjoy swimming, and I particularly like hiking. I enjoy being out on a trail, exploring a new route, and spending time away from screens and coursework.
I also enjoy discovering new places. Whether it is exploring a new part of the city, visiting somewhere I have never been before, or simply taking a different route and seeing what I find, I like the experience of discovering something new.
I am a big cricket fan and enjoy following and watching cricket whenever I get the chance. It has been one of my favourite ways to unwind and stay connected with something I have enjoyed for years.
In my quieter time, I enjoy listening to music and watching movies. These are usually how I relax after a busy day and take a break from academics.
I also really enjoy meeting new people. Moving to a new country has given me the opportunity to meet people from different backgrounds, hear their stories, and make new connections. For me, these experiences are an important part of life outside the classroom.
